FrequencyLab

web · FLOW perceptual model

What this app is for

FrequencyLab is a tool for designing haptic music — particularly polyphony — built from two superimposed vibrations (sinusoids) delivered through a single actuator. It shows you which pairs of frequencies fuse into a single vibration and which split apart into two separate perceptual streams, and what frequency (or frequencies) you'd actually perceive in each case.

Perceptual space (left canvas)

The main plot is the perceptual space for a pair of frequencies f1 and f2. The background shading is the model's prediction of the percentage of trials perceived as two vibrations rather than one, across the whole space. Hover or click anywhere to try a pair, or click one of the outlined dots directly — those dots are real behavioural data points from psychophysical testing, not simulated.

Perception dial

The dial compares the model's prediction (white) against the real behavioural data (red, shown once you click an existing data point) for the same quantity: the likelihood of perceiving two vibrations instead of one.

The model

A linear model with a common slope for Grassy Hill and Beat stimuli explained 72.1% of the variance in double-vibration responses, with a highly significant slope relating FS–ENV spacing to the likelihood of perceiving two vibrations (β = 20.42, p < .001). The class-by-spacing interaction was not significant (β = 1.158, p = .785), confirming that the two classes share a single slope once expressed on this common axis. The two regression lines are therefore parallel, differing only in intercept: Beat stimuli show a significant upward offset of 9.71 percentage points relative to Grassy Hill (p = .013) at any given level of FS–ENV separation.

Beat:   y = 20.42x + 8.84
Grassy Hill:   y = 20.42x − 0.86

As a single equation:
y = 20.42x − 0.86 + 9.71·𝟙Beat
where 𝟙Beat = 1 for Beat stimuli and 0 for Grassy Hill

Perceived identity

The readout's "Perceived frequency" line tells you which frequency (or frequencies) you'd actually perceive, per this model: when one vibration is perceived, it's the geometric mean of the two components; when two are perceived, they're the envelope (ENV) and fine-structure (FS) frequencies separately.

TouchSim panel (bottom)

Below, the TouchSim panel shows a simulated peripheral neural response (Saal, Delhaye, Rayhaun & Bensmaia, 2017 — see References) to the stimulus: a raster of afferent spike times and the autocorrelation/periodicity spectrum of that spiking, showing which frequencies (ENV, FS, and harmonics) are actually encoded in the nervous system's response.
